items.title: 61539_Butter Jackson oral history interview
items.q: So Clark and I left at the same time.

ctx.x: That was 1959. I left him in October and Quincy came over in November. So Clark and I left at the same time. You know, Clark, he used to say all the time, 'I'm going to -- I'll bet I'll be here -- I bet I'll leave before you will.' I said, 'No, you won't.' So we wound up leaving together. And we stayed over in Europe until Quincy came and that's when I made a little record that --

items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Finally I found out that Quentin Jackson – Butter, we called him – was a good buddy. I would say, “Hey Butter, excuse me Butter, what tunes are we playing?”

ctx.x: How was the – what was the – how was it like, breaking into the band on a personal level?

It was a very, very difficult thing, to break into that band on a personal level, because they were not very friendly people at all times, particularly to new people coming in the band. They used to have a saying there: “don’t put your laundry in ’til you’ve even been there a while.” I would very often wonder what tunes we would play, because Duke never called a tune. He never announced it. He would indicate what was being played through the medium of the introduction which he played on the tune. He would go…
Did the – how much of that band was on the paper? How much was in those guys heads?
